title: In a Changing Los Angeles, Thank God for the SoCal Beach Dive Bar
summary: Old, briny watering holes in the city and its surrounding counties are keeping a decades-long legacy alive.
content:
Los Angeles is the artistic and financial hub of Southern California. But at the same time, my hometown and its surrounding counties are rapidly losing their identity. Film and television production began to flee in the late ’90s, and it has only gotten worse over the last 30 years: Wildfires have increased 30-fold over the last four decades, and ICE raids have terrorized the vibrant immigrant communities that make up the fabric of our interconnected cities. Hell, we can’t even brag that “at least it’s a dry heat” anymore. 

But at least one legacy, thank god, remains: The SoCal Beach Dive Bar. You know them when you see them. In Southern California, stretching from Imperial Beach and the Tijuana border on the south end, up to somewhere in Santa Barbara County (the northern dividing line is not official), coastal towns are littered with them: the kinds of breezy bars filled with flip-flop degenerates of all economic standings, knocking back pitchers of domestic beer and perhaps a flattop-griddled cheese burger with a side of potato chips. These salty saloons—some dating back to the early 1900s—are not necessarily on the beach. Thanks to consistently escalating land values, the best of these bars are often within smelling distance of the sea, but a few minutes’ walk from those pricier shores. You can feel the beach in these places, even if you can’t see it. These old briny watering holes are for people who want to be near the ocean, even if they haven’t stepped into it for months or maybe a decade.

Here is how you know you’re in a SoCal Beach Dive Bar: The decor is often tiki-adjacent (the tiki bar was invented in Hollywood, by the way), or nautical in nature. Sometimes, like at The Harbor Room in Playa del Rey, or The Galley in Santa Monica, it might feel like you’re drinking in the belly of an old wooden ship. Old wood is a plus, so are places without credit card machines (though these are getting more and more rare).

title: All the Ways to Coffee Your Cocktail
summary: An updated guide to the recipes and techniques to wake up your next round.
content:
“It’s a transitional drink,” says Tristan Willey, co-founder of Good Vodka, of the Espresso Martini. This is true of all coffee cocktails, whether that transition is from day to night with that monster of a drink, or, as the seasons change, from refreshing, warm-weather coffee cocktails to warming one’s hands with a steaming cup of espresso-based Livorno Punch. 

There is more than one way to caffeinate your cocktail. Here are our favorites.

For the most potent dose of fresh coffee flavor, turn to espresso. The Espresso Martini is an obvious choice to feature the brew; while modern recipes call for cold brew or flavored liqueur, all three of our favorite recipes in a tasting of several versions stuck with espresso. 

For the easiest espresso-plus-booze combinations, turn to the caffeinated cocktails of history. There’s the Mexico City party drink that hails from the 19th century, the carajillo, made by pouring espresso and the Licor 43 over ice. And even before that, there was the 17th-century protococktail from Italy, Livorno Punch, a steamy combination of espresso, spiced rum, sugar and a lemon twist.

title: Our Favorite Easy Nonalcoholic Cocktails
summary: An updated guide for Sober October or whenever you want an N/A drink.
content:
Nonalcoholic cocktails have come a long way. By now, you know that the category is more than just cloying fruit punches, and that “mocktail” is no longer a dirty word; go to any good cocktail bar and you’ll find more than one creative N/A drink that’s just as celebratory as its full-proof counterparts.

Here are our favorite nonalcoholic cocktail recipes. Some turn the classics—Negroni to Espresso Martini—spirit-free. But others take a different tact. As bartender, author and N/A drinks fan John deBary puts it, a growing number of bars are “breaking free from the familiar—and useful—beats of cocktail orthodoxy” to make their mocktails. Sometimes it’s more exciting to make something entirely brand new.

title: The Most Popular Cocktails of September
summary: Here are the drinks that you couldn’t get enough of this month.
content: How do we know it’s fall? There’s rye in the mixing glasses and maple syrup in the jiggers. There’s cocktails channeling the smell of a rainy day, stiff Martinis making their seasonal debut, and home bartenders clamoring for the honeyed herbal flavor of yellow Chartreuse. If you’re in the autumnal mood, a great place to start would be to make the drinks our readers loved most in September. Get all the recipes below.

title: Who Wants to Go to the Punk Show at the Dumpling Shop?
summary: 3rd Space is turning unconventional locations into concert venues, from an underground show at a dim sum lounge to an electronic set at a midtown Manhattan heliport.
content:
I feel a lot of FOMO that I haven’t yet gotten to go to one of the concerts put on by 3rd Space, hosts of such spectacles as the Asian underground show at a dim sum lounge, the electronic set at a midtown Manhattan heliport, or the evening of harps and clarinets at a community garden. In an era of stunt-y dinner parties and corporate sponsors going rogue with experiential budgets, a cynic might say these are gimmicks. But I don’t see it that way. These days, apparently people don’t know how to dance at the club, or even how to put their phones down for a night to actually let loose. As Spencer Papandrea, 3rd Space’s founder, sees it, being intentional about his shows’ settings helps concertgoers fully immerse themselves, and that makes the experience so much better. Here’s how he and the team produce events.

This is an excerpt from Pre Shift, our newsletter for bartenders, restaurant workers and the hospitality industry. Subscribe for more perspectives like this in your inbox.

title: Five Underrated Gin Cocktails
summary: From a tropical fizz to an unsung Martini and more.
content:
Between the bar world’s enduring Martini madness and the fact that Negronis can now be found in every flavor, from rhubarb to panettone, the gin classics are hardly underdogs. Still, the canon has its hidden gems, whether it’s long-lost aperitivi or “minor classics.” Here are five to know.

First served for a visiting cardinal in Rome in 1950 (hence the name), the original Cardinale combined gin, white wine and Campari. Today, the wine is often swapped out for dry vermouth, which makes it “more austere and bone-dry,” according to bartender Naren Young, whose own version calls on Contratto Bitter. Another variation on the lesser-known aperitivo drink, meanwhile, is tall and sparkling thanks to Campari Soda, an Italian RTD.

title: How Indigenous Restaurants Build Their Drink Menus
summary: Chefs contend with the history of industrialized alcohol—and the misconceptions and stigma around it—while designing their bar programs.
content:
When he opened his progressive Indigenous restaurant Naagan in Ontario, Canada, in late 2024, Ojibwe chef Zach Keeshig knew that he wouldn’t serve wine, beer or spirits. The alcohol-related death rate among Native people in North America remains three to five times higher than the general population’s—statistics that, for Keeshig, are hardly abstract. He’d seen many people close to him succumb to alcoholism. His own father had recently died, “sitting by himself, drinking.” Moreover, Keeshig wanted to “tell the story of what Indigenous food could be,” and like white flour, processed sugar and other ingredients he’d omitted from Naagan’s kitchen, alcohol was not part of the pre-contact Indigenous diet. For many North American Indigenous chefs, alcohol presents a conundrum: Bar programs are cash cows and it’s tough to run an upscale restaurant without one, but what kind of bar program makes sense in an Indigenous restaurant?

Let’s get this out of the way: The theory that Native peoples have some biological weakness to alcohol has been soundly debunked. Historically, that theory has functioned as a convenient blame-shifter, used as “proof” that Natives simply can’t hold their liquor, and that “the problems Natives face have nothing to do with settler violence,” says Michael D. Wise, author of Native Foods: Agriculture, Indigeneity, and Settler Colonialism in American History. “Alcohol is this deus ex machina force that absolves American settlers.” 

Although for millennia, Indigenous peoples brewed fermented drinks and ingested mind-altering substances, particularly in ceremony, it was European settlers and their descendants who industrialized alcohol, bringing beer to the Americas, introducing Vitis vinifera for wine and eventually distilling spirits. By the late 1800s, the federal governments of the United States and Canada had forced hundreds of thousands of Native people off their ancestral homelands, disrupted their food sovereignty and herded them onto reservations. Most Indigenous people today live in urban and suburban environments, but those who remain in tribal communities (about 20 percent in the United States and 40 percent in Canada) contend with a slew of alcohol-abuse risk factors, including remoteness, lack of resources, stigma and poverty. “Environments in which Native people live expose them to PTSD-qualifying events (death, threatened death, actual or threatened serious injury, or actual or threatened sexual violence) far more frequently than the environments of their non-Indian counterparts,” says Spero Manson, director of the Centers for American Indian & Alaska Native Health at Colorado School of Public Health. “We’re talking 60-70 percent of individuals living in tribal communities being exposed to serious trauma.”

In Indigenous restaurants, alcohol is not neutral, so some chefs serve it with caveats. “We don’t mix alcohol with medicine,” says Inez Cook of First Nations restaurant Salmon n’ Bannock in Vancouver, British Columbia. She reserves traditionally medicinal ingredients like sweetgrass and sage for mocktails. In cocktails, she showcases hard-to-come-by Indigenous ingredients, including soopolallie, or soap berries. When she can source soopolallie, she whips it into a foam to garnish a blend of orange juice, sparkling water, vodka and “Bella Coola tea” prepared with berries, rosehips, hibiscus and maple.

For Cree chef Shane Chartrand, dinners at his restaurant Paperbirch in Alberta, Canada, aren’t ceremonial. “There’s no smudging or land acknowledgement or anything,” he says. “This is just the culinary arts. It’s just dinner.” Because of that, though he’s sober himself, he feels comfortable offering local mead, beer and wine. He also acknowledges the demand for alcoholic beverages. “I can only be as Indigenous as the world allows me to be at a dinner where people are paying $120,” he says. Choctaw chef David Skinner of Ishtia in Kemah, Texas, concurs: “We don’t add alcohol to any of the food,” says, “but if you’re spending a couple hundred dollars and three hours of your life in a restaurant, you’re going to want a glass of wine or a cocktail.” 

It’s true that they are going to want it. But they also might act suspicious about it: Although Natives in the food and beverage space are expected to supply booze, doing so subjects them to stereotypes. As Chiricahua Apache Nde and Rarámuri brewer and distiller Roxanne Fernandez Tiburolobo told Punch in 2021, “I’ve had people that I brewed with be like, ‘Oh, you’re native? I didn’t know you people could have alcohol.’”

title: How to Use Génépy in Cocktails
summary: An updated guide to the bracing herbal liqueur, a close cousin of Chartreuse, which adds an alpine twist to any drink.
content:
Just five years ago, génépy (or genepi, as it is more commonly called in Italy) remained fairly unknown outside its native Europe. The herbal liqueur—made by steeping its same-named plant génépy, aka artemisia, in neutral alcohol—has long been a staple of après-ski traditions, often served neat or simply topped with tonic. Today, as the category continues to grow stateside—including with domestically made expressions—génépy has graduated from alpine obscurity to backbar staple, becoming a popular go-to in cocktails for a hit of herbal complexity without the intensity, or scarcity, of its cousin Chartreuse.

Génépy is not as sweet as yellow Chartreuse, nor as domineering as green, and it adds a cooling complexity to everything from Margaritas to Whiskey Sours to White Negronis. In the Petrichor, Nikki Irvine uses génépy to translate the earthy smell after to rain into a drink, while Toby Maloney describes the Swiss Kiss, which marries gin, génépy and lemon juice and a float of absinthe, as being “as cool and sophisticated as a Swiss diplomat at a party of spies.”

At San Francisco’s ABV, bar staff are known to drink ice-cold génépy topped with a few dashes of Angostura bitters. There, Ryan Fitzgerald blended it into the High Altitude Highball, made with Japanese whisky, namely Hakushu, with génépy and soda water. “Both Hakushu and génépy come from mountain areas—and both are influenced by the region they come from,” he says. 

Finally, the alpine ingredient works well alongside comforting, cozy flavors like coffee and cacao.  “One of my favorite uses for génépy is as a sweetener for heavy cream,” says Troy Sidle, former bartender at New York’s Pouring Ribbons. In the Strong Start, he shakes the two ingredients together with a pinch of salt for a frothy, aromatic topper to the rum-spiked coffee. Ryan Maybee, on the other hand, brings cream and coffee cordial together with the liqueur, crème de cacao and absinthe for the Génépy Suisse. The extra wintry drink channels an elevated, adult mocha. “The sweeter qualities of the cacao and coffee blend beautifully with absinthe, and work equally well with génépy,” he says.

title: Our Favorite Easy Whiskey Cocktails
summary: Go beyond the classic Manhattan and Old-Fashioned with these simple recipes that require just a few ingredients.
content: The whiskey classics—Old-Fashioned to Manhattan—need no introduction. But there are plenty of riffs on those time-tested drinks, along with original cocktails made with the spirit, that deserve a place in your recipe rotation. Here, we’ve collected some of our favorites that are as easy to make as the whiskey staples you know and love. From a two-part rye and damson liqueur drink to a bourbon and fernet favorite, here’s what you should be making this season.

title: Time to Tackle a Cocktail Project
summary: Here's how to master at-home clarification, fermentation, force carbonation and more.
content:
Like any practice, there are levels to at-home bartending. Stocking up on the best tools, spirits for mixing and classic recipes may be one tier of mastery, but building an entire carbonation rig in your kitchen is probably the ultimate home bar flex. If you’ve nailed the easy cocktail projects, it’s time to take things up a notch. Here are five next-level cocktail projects to try.

First employed in the famous Benton’s Old-Fashioned at PDT in 2007, fat-washing has evolved to encompass a whole wave of spirit-infusion techniques. At its simplest, fat-washing requires melting a fat—say, coconut oil or animal fat—infusing it into a spirit, freezing the mixture, then straining out the solids for a bolder, fuller-bodied flavor. Try the technique with coconut oil, chile oil and even peanut butter.

title: I Went to a “Fight Your Evil Situationship Boxing Rave”
summary: Everyone says Gen Z doesn’t party. I went to the ring to see if we can (physically) beat the allegations.
content:
“Forgive me, baby,” pleaded a shirtless boxer through a spittle-filled mouthguard to their ex-lover. The crowd’s boos echoed through thick fake smoke.

For years, Gen Z has been pigeonholed as the inside generation. Allegedly, Gen Z is lonely; Gen Z doesn’t dance or party or go to bars. I, a 24-year-old living in Brooklyn, have been sent to a “Fight Your Evil Situationship” Boxing Rave to see if this is what we do instead.

Walking upstairs into a cavernous, smoky room filled with my peers—clad in all haircuts and jean leg widths—I felt the bass before I saw the ring. I don’t know what I was expecting when I first came across the flyer for the event, which sought “fighters that will bring a slight horniness,” but it wasn’t an actual boxing ring. There it was, though, with ropes and strobe lights delineating the edges, and a DJ booth behind it. That was the least of the surprises of the night. 

Grownkid, the host of this event, is a “social club for 18- to 24-year-olds” started by Gael Aitor and Kayla Suarez. This is not the duo’s first foray into fight-centric partying; for Valentine’s Day this year, they held a wrestling speed dating night. And this very physical means of closeness—from modern medieval combat to lesbian oil wrestling to the (now mainstream, or at least corporatized) Twinks vs. Dolls showdown—has also been on the rise. In the same city, on the same weekend, Migo Events scheduled its Lucha Libre, promising freestyle wrestling and mariscos at a skate park.
